summary: Tutankhamun took 413 little servants into the afterlife: a worker for every day of the year, plus foremen with whips to keep them at it.
look: Rows of small mummy-shaped figures in gilded wood, blue faience and stone, most between the length of your hand and your forearm. Many hold a hoe and a pick, or have a basket on the back, ready for field work. A few look different: men dressed as the living, in a kilt, holding a whip. Those are the overseers.
story:
The Egyptian afterlife was not a holiday. The Field of Reeds looked like a perfect Egypt, and a perfect Egypt still had fields to plough and canals to clear. From the Middle Kingdom onwards the answer was a stand-in: a figure inscribed with a spell that steps forward when the gods call the dead person up for labour. The spell became Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead, and its key line is the figure's reply: 'I will do it, here I am.' The word changed over the centuries, shabti, shawabti, ushabti, and scholars still argue whether it meant 'answerer'.

Carter counted 413 in Tutankhamun's tomb, most in the Annexe and the Treasury, packed in black shrine-shaped boxes with miniature tools of copper and faience. The usual reading of the number is neat: 365 workers, one per day, 36 overseers, one for each gang of ten, and 12 more, one for each month.

Not all came from the royal workshop. Some carry dedications from powerful men at court, the general Nakhtmin and the treasurer Maya among them. A gift to the dead king was also a way of being seen at his funeral. The finest figures are small portrait sculptures with the king's full cheeks and heavy-lidded eyes.
details: The overseers: figures in a kilt, as living men, often with a whip. Count how few they are next to the workers.
Miniature hoes, picks and baskets in copper and faience, made for the shabtis to work with.
Horizontal bands of text round the legs: usually the shabti spell, Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead.
Compare materials: gilded wood, blue faience, dark stone, pale calcite. The best are true portraits of the king.
A few carry a short line naming the giver, such as the general Nakhtmin. Check the labels.
fun_fact: One overseer for every ten workers, and a dozen monthly bosses on top: Tutankhamun's afterlife farm came with middle management.
narration: These little mummy-shaped figures are Tutankhamun's workforce for eternity. The Egyptian afterlife looked like a perfect Egypt, and a perfect Egypt still needed fields ploughed and canals cleared. So people took stand-ins. Each figure carries a spell, Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead. When the gods call the dead man to work, the figure answers: I will do it, here I am. That may be where the name comes from, ushabti, the answerer, though scholars still argue. Howard Carter counted 413 of them. The neat reading is 365 workers, one for every day of the year, 36 overseers, one for every gang of ten, and 12 more, one for each month. Most were packed in black boxes in the Annexe and the Treasury, with tiny tools of copper and faience. Not all came from the palace. Some were gifts from powerful men at court, like the general Nakhtmin and the treasurer Maya, a way of being seen at the king's funeral. Look now for the odd ones out: figures in a kilt, dressed as living men, holding a whip. Those are the bosses.

summary: Gilded figures sealed in black shrines: the king striding on a leopard, the king spearing an invisible hippo, and a crowd of gods to escort him.
look: Gold-covered wooden figures, most well under a metre tall, standing on black bases. Find the king walking on the back of a black leopard, and the king on a little papyrus boat with a harpoon raised. Around them stand gilded gods and goddesses, some with the king's own face.
story:
In the Treasury, Carter found a row of black wooden chests shaped like shrines, their doors tied shut and sealed. Inside, each gilded statuette stood wrapped in linen, as if dressed for a journey. Together they are a cast for the king's night voyage through the underworld.

Two figures show the king in the White Crown striding along the back of a black leopard. The same image is painted in the tomb of Seti II, so it belonged to the royal underworld, not to a hunting trip; the cat may stand for the dark realm the king must cross. Two more show him on a papyrus skiff, arm raised, a coil of rope in the other hand. The target is missing on purpose. In temple reliefs it is a hippopotamus, the animal of Seth, god of chaos. Here the enemy is left to your imagination.

The gods include Ptah, with Tutankhamun's features, Sekhmet, Duamutef, one of the four sons of Horus, and the goddess Menkaret carrying the small king on her head. Not everything was made for him. Some Egyptologists point to one leopard figure with a soft, almost female chest and argue it was first made for Neferneferuaten, the mysterious ruler before him, then reused.
details: The leopard figures: a black cat, a gilded king in the tall White Crown. Compare the two chests; one looks softer, almost female.
The harpooner: rope coiled in one hand, harpoon raised in the other, and no hippo anywhere. That is deliberate.
Ptah, wrapped tight like a mummy, with Tutankhamun's face.
Menkaret, a goddess carrying a small figure of the king on her head.
The black shrine-shaped chests, if shown: each figure was sealed inside one.
fun_fact: When the shrines were opened, the gilded figures were found wrapped in linen like passengers in travelling cloaks.
narration: Here is the king's escort for the night journey. In the Treasury, Howard Carter found a row of black wooden chests shaped like little shrines, all sealed. Inside stood gilded figures, each wrapped in linen like a traveller in a cloak. Start with the leopard. The king, in the tall White Crown, strides along the back of a black cat. It is not a hunting trophy. The same image is painted in the tomb of Seti the Second, so it belongs to the underworld, perhaps the dark realm the king had to cross. Some Egyptologists think one of the two leopard figures, with its soft, almost female chest, was first made for Neferneferuaten, the mysterious ruler before Tutankhamun. Then the harpooner: the king on a papyrus skiff, arm raised, rope coiled in his hand. His target is missing on purpose. In temple scenes it is a hippopotamus, the creature of Seth, god of chaos. Here the enemy is left to your imagination. Around him stand the gods, Ptah with the king's own face, Sekhmet and more. Look now at the empty water before the harpooner.

summary: A gold fan shows the king hunting the very ostriches whose feathers it once held, and 130 sticks raise the question: did Tutankhamun limp?
look: The gold fan is a half-round head on a long handle, with holes along the curved edge where ostrich feathers were fixed; the feathers have mostly perished. One face shows the king hunting ostriches from his chariot, the other his return with the catch. Nearby are walking sticks: plain reeds, gilded canes, and canes whose curved handles are bound foreign captives.
story:
The fan was found between the gilded shrines in the burial chamber. Its inscription says the feathers came from ostriches the king hunted himself in the desert near Heliopolis, so the gold tells the fan's own origin story.

The sticks are a puzzle. More than 130 canes and staffs went into the tomb, one labelled as a reed His Majesty cut with his own hand. When a 2010 DNA study suggested a clubfoot, the canes were offered as proof that he limped. A later study found very little wear on them, and canes were also badges of rank. The jury is still out.
details: Fan, hunting side: the king draws his bow from a racing chariot as ostriches flee.
Fan, other side: servants carry the dead birds home; the king holds the plumes under his arm.
The holes along the fan's curved edge, where the feathers were fixed.
Canes with handles carved as bound foreign captives: the king held his enemies in his hand.
fun_fact: The fan is a souvenir of its own making: the gold shows the hunt that supplied its feathers.
narration: This gold fan tells its own origin story. On one face the young king races his chariot and draws his bow at fleeing ostriches. On the other, servants carry the birds home and the king holds the plumes under his arm. The inscription says the feathers came from his own hunt in the desert near Heliopolis. The feathers have mostly perished, but you can see the holes where they were fixed. Now the sticks. More than 130 canes and staffs were buried with him. After a DNA study suggested a clubfoot, people said: there is the proof he limped. A later study found the sticks show very little wear, and canes were badges of rank. Look now for the canes whose handles are bound foreign captives.

summary: A small gold shrine covered in tender scenes of a teenage king and queen. The statue it was made for was stolen over 3,000 years ago.
look: A wooden shrine about half a metre tall, sheathed in gold and set on a sledge, with a roof sloping down towards the back like the ancient shrine of Upper Egypt. Every outside panel shows Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun together. Walk all the way round and read it like a comic strip.
story:
Carter found it in the Antechamber. Inside was a base for a small statue, but the statue itself was gone, taken by robbers soon after the funeral. They missed a necklace with a pendant of Weret-Hekau, 'Great of Magic', a snake goddess with a woman's head, nursing the king.

The panels are some of the most intimate royal images from ancient Egypt. Ankhesenamun hands her husband arrows as he shoots at birds from a seat. She ties a collar round his neck, offers him flowers, and perfume passes between their hands. She was his wife and probably his half-sister, a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, born Ankhesenpaaten.

These are not holiday snapshots. The queen plays the role of goddesses such as Hathor and Weret-Hekau, who renew the king's power and promise new life, so the shrine is about kingship and fertility as much as love. Still, the soft, curving lines are the Amarna style the couple grew up with, and they make two teenagers look like real people.
details: The panel where the king sits shooting at birds and the queen holds out an arrow.
The queen fastening a broad collar round the king's neck.
Scenes where perfume or water passes between their hands: who serves whom changes from panel to panel.
The cartouches of king and queen in the text columns framing each scene.
If the doors are open: the empty base where the stolen statue once stood.
fun_fact: Ankhesenamun means 'She lives for Amun'. She was born Ankhesenpaaten, 'She lives for the Aten', and changed her name when the court abandoned her father's god.
narration: This small shrine of gold is the closest thing to a family album that Tutankhamun left. Every panel shows the young king with his queen, Ankhesenamun, probably his half-sister and a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti. Walk around it slowly. She hands him arrows as he shoots at birds from a seat. She ties a collar round his neck. She offers him flowers. Perfume passes between their hands. Howard Carter found the shrine in the Antechamber. Inside was a base for a small statue, but the statue was gone, stolen soon after the funeral. The robbers missed a necklace showing a snake goddess called Great of Magic, nursing the king. That is the key. These are not holiday snapshots. The queen plays goddesses like Hathor, who renew the king's power and promise new life. Still, the soft curving lines are the Amarna style they grew up with, and they make two teenagers look real. Look now for the panel where she holds out an arrow and he draws his bow.

summary: Royal clothes almost never survive from ancient Egypt. Tutankhamun's tomb kept his tunics, his gloves and a pile of linen underwear.
look: Folded linen garments behind glass: a tunic with woven and embroidered bands at the neck and hem, small linen gloves, sashes, and triangular loincloths with ties. The linen is brown and brittle now. Imagine it bright white, with coloured borders.
story:
Egyptian art shows kings in crisp white linen, but real royal clothes almost never survive. Tutankhamun's tomb is the exception. Carter found hundreds of textiles, many stuffed back into boxes by officials who tidied up after ancient robbers: tunics, kilts, shirts, sashes, gloves and around 145 loincloths.

The showpieces are tunics with tapestry-woven and embroidered decoration; Carter nicknamed one ceremonial robe a 'dalmatic', after a church vestment. Gloves may have been for gripping a chariot's reins. Some pieces are small enough for a boy, as if clothes from his childhood were kept and buried with him.
details: The tunic's neck opening and hem: woven bands and embroidery in coloured thread.
The gloves: linen, sized for a young man's hands, perhaps for driving a chariot.
Triangular loincloths with ties: the basic underwear of ancient Egypt.
The brown colour: linen darkens with age. It was once white.
fun_fact: Around 145 loincloths went into the tomb. Even a god-king needed clean underwear for eternity.
narration: Here is something almost nothing else in Egypt can show you: a king's actual clothes. Paintings show pharaohs in crisp white linen, but real royal garments almost never survive. Tutankhamun's tomb kept hundreds of textiles, many stuffed back into boxes by officials tidying up after ancient robbers. There are tunics with woven and embroidered borders, sashes, gloves that may have been for driving a chariot, and around 145 loincloths. Some pieces are small enough for a boy, as if clothes from his childhood were kept. The linen has turned brown with age. Imagine it bright white. Look now at the gloves, and at how small those hands were.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BC; tomb found 1922
summary: The gold is here, but the king is not. His mummy and his stone sarcophagus are still in KV62 in the Valley of the Kings.
look: Nothing to look at in this gallery: this entry explains the split. On 21 October, in the burial chamber of KV62, you will see what stayed: the quartzite sarcophagus with a winged goddess at each corner, the mummy in a glass case, and the painted walls. The outermost gilded coffin also stayed in the tomb until July 2019, when it came to the Grand Egyptian Museum for restoration, to be shown with the other two.
story:
When Carter cleared the tomb, between 1922 and 1932, nearly everything went to Cairo. The king stayed, in his quartzite sarcophagus, whose lid was replaced by glass, inside his outermost coffin. Since 4 November 2007 the mummy has lain in a climate-controlled glass case in the tomb.

It is not a pretty story. In November 1925 the anatomist Douglas Derry unwrapped the body. Resins had glued it to the gold coffin, so the team chiselled it out, used hot knives to free the head from the mask, cut the torso at the hips and took the arms apart. It went back to the tomb on a tray of sand in 1926. When R. G. Harrison X-rayed it in 1968, parts of the chest were missing, probably taken by thieves after the reburial.

A CT scan in 2005 confirmed an age of about 19, ruled out the old theory of a fatal blow to the head, and found a leg fracture that never healed. A DNA study published in 2010 named the KV55 mummy, probably Akhenaten, as his father and the 'Younger Lady' from KV35 as his mother, found malaria parasites, and proposed malaria plus the fracture as the cause of death. Other experts dispute parts of the genetics and the clubfoot diagnosis: it is the best current guess.
details: In the tomb, north wall: Ay, the next king, performs the Opening of the Mouth on Tutankhamun's mummy.
East wall: the funeral procession dragging the coffin, a private-tomb scene found in no other royal tomb.
West wall: twelve baboons from the Amduat, the book of the sun's night journey.
The sarcophagus: quartzite box, red granite lid painted to match, goddesses spreading their wings at the corners.
If the real tomb is crowded, a full-size replica of the burial chamber was opened near Carter's house in 2014.
fun_fact: The king was found with 143 objects tucked into his wrappings, from amulets to two daggers, one with a blade of meteoric iron.
narration: Nothing in this gallery is the king himself, and that is the point of this stop. When Howard Carter emptied the tomb, almost everything came to Cairo, but the mummy and the stone sarcophagus stayed in K V 62 in the Valley of the Kings, where you will see them on the 21st. The mummy's story is rough. In November 1925 the anatomist Douglas Derry unwrapped it. Resins had glued the body to the gold coffin, so the team chiselled it out, used hot knives to free the head from the mask, and cut the body into pieces. It went back into the tomb on a tray of sand. A CT scan in 2005 put his age at about 19, ruled out the old theory of a blow to the head, and found a broken leg that never healed. In 2010 a DNA study named the K V 55 mummy, probably Akhenaten, as his father, found malaria, and suggested malaria plus the fracture as the cause of death. Other experts dispute parts of it, so call it the best current guess. When you stand in the tomb, look for Ay on the north wall, performing the last rites for the king.

period: Late Predynastic to 1st Dynasty, c. 3100 BC
summary: A make-up palette far too big to use, carved around 3100 BC with a king smiting his enemy: the pose every pharaoh copied for 3,000 years.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. If you find it: a shield-shaped slab of dark grey-green siltstone about 63 cm tall, carved on both faces. One side shows the king in the tall White Crown, mace raised over a kneeling captive. The other has two long-necked beasts whose necks curl round a shallow circle: the grinding dish.
story:
In the 1897-98 season James Quibell and Frederick Green were digging at Hierakonpolis, ancient Nekhen, a centre of the falcon god Horus; the Greek name means 'falcon city'. In a buried cache of old temple offerings, the 'Main Deposit', they found this palette. Palettes were normally small slabs for grinding eye paint. This one is too big and heavy for any dressing table. It was a temple gift, perhaps used to grind cosmetics for a god's statue.

At the top of both sides the king's name sits in a palace-façade box: a catfish and a chisel, read Nar-mer, between cow heads usually identified as the goddess Bat. On one side Narmer, in the White Crown of Upper Egypt, raises a mace over a kneeling enemy, while a falcon holds a captive head rising from a papyrus marsh on a rope and a servant carries the king's sandals. On the other side, in the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, he marches to view ten beheaded enemies, each head placed between the feet. Below, two serpopards, leopards with snake necks, are held on leashes. At the bottom a bull, the king, smashes a walled town.

For a century this was read as a news report: the south conquers the north, Egypt is united. Many Egyptologists now see it less as one event than as a statement of what kings do: crush disorder, rule both lands. Either way, the smiting pose lasted until the Roman emperors.
details: Top of both sides: catfish and chisel in a box, Narmer's name, flanked by cow heads with curling horns.
Smiting side: the small sandal-bearer behind the king, carrying his sandals.
Other side, top right: ten headless bodies laid in rows, each head between its feet.
The serpopards: long-necked beasts on leashes, their necks framing the grinding dish.
The king's belt: tassels capped with little cow-goddess heads, and a bull's tail hanging behind.
fun_fact: Narmer wears a bull's tail hanging from his belt. Pharaohs kept wearing one for the next 3,000 years.
narration: If you have found it, you are looking at the slab where Egyptian kingship begins. The Narmer Palette was carved about 3100 BC from dark siltstone, and found in the 1890s by James Quibell and Frederick Green at Hierakonpolis, a Greek name meaning city of the falcon, in a buried pile of old temple offerings. Palettes were small slabs for grinding eye paint. This one is far too big for any dressing table. It was a gift to a god. At the top of both faces, between two cow heads, is the king's name in a little box: a catfish and a chisel, read Nar and Mer. On one side Narmer wears the tall White Crown of the south and raises a mace over a kneeling enemy, held by the hair. Behind him a servant carries his sandals. On the other side he wears the Red Crown of the north and marches to inspect ten headless enemies, each head placed between the feet. Below, two monsters with leopard bodies and snake necks curl around the dish where paint was ground. At the bottom, a bull, the king himself, smashes a walled town. For a century people read this as the unification of Egypt in one war. Many Egyptologists now see it as a statement of what kings do. Either way, that smiting pose lasted 3,000 years, and you will see Ramesses doing the same at Abu Simbel. Look now for the catfish at the top.

summary: The builder of the second Giza pyramid, sitting in stone so hard it barely takes a chisel, with the falcon god folding its wings round his head.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A life-size seated king, about 1.68 m tall, in dark stone flecked with pale crystals. From the front you see a calm man in the striped nemes headcloth and false beard. Now walk to the side: a falcon perches on the back of the throne and wraps its wings round the back of his head.
story:
Auguste Mariette found the statue in 1860 in Khafre's valley temple at Giza, the granite building beside the Sphinx that you visit on the 12th. It had been thrown into a pit in the temple. The temple's hall has sockets in the floor for 23 statues of the king; this is the one that survived whole.

The stone matters. It is anorthosite gneiss, often loosely called diorite, brought from the 'Khafre quarries' deep in the Nubian desert west of Gebel el-Asr, about 1,000 km up the Nile from Giza. It is extremely hard, so every smooth curve was won by grinding with abrasive sand.

Now read the composition. The throne's sides are lions. Between the legs, the lily of the south and the papyrus of the north are tied around the hieroglyph for 'unite': this king holds the Two Lands together. The falcon is Horus, and the king is Horus on earth. From the front you hardly notice the bird; from the side, king and god become one being.

Khafre is the Chephren of Herodotus, who heard that he and his father Khufu closed the temples and were so hated that Egyptians avoided saying their names. This face does not look like a tyrant. It is an ideal, calm and ageless, a permanent home for the king's ka, the life-force that needed a body that would never decay.
details: The falcon: walk to the side and look behind the king's head. Its wings wrap round the back of the nemes.
The throne sides: lion legs, and the lily and papyrus knotted together, the sign of the united Two Lands.
His hands: the right is clenched, the left lies flat on his knee.
The stone: dark gneiss with pale flecks, from a Nubian quarry about 1,000 km to the south.
fun_fact: In the Valley Temple on the 12th, you can still see the sockets in the floor where 23 statues of Khafre once sat. You have just met the survivor.
narration: If you have found him, you are looking at Khafre, king of the second pyramid at Giza, whose face most Egyptologists see on the Sphinx. He sits life-size in stone so hard it barely takes a chisel. Auguste Mariette found him in 1860 in Khafre's valley temple, the granite building beside the Sphinx that you will walk through on the 12th. He had been thrown into a pit. The floor of that temple has sockets for 23 statues of the king; this is the one that survived whole. The stone is anorthosite gneiss, often called diorite, dark with pale flecks. It came from quarries deep in the Nubian desert, about 1,000 kilometres up the Nile, and every smooth curve was ground with sand. Now walk slowly to the side. A falcon perches on the back of the throne and folds its wings round the king's head. That is Horus, and the king is Horus on earth. From the front you hardly see the bird. From the side, king and god become one. Look at the throne too: lions for legs, and the lily of the south and the papyrus of the north tied together, the sign for a united Egypt. The Greeks called him Chephren, and Herodotus heard that he was a tyrant who shut the temples. This face does not look like a tyrant. It is an ideal, calm and ageless, a home for the king's spirit forever. Look now for the falcon's wings behind his headcloth.

summary: The owner of the smallest Giza pyramid stands with the goddess Hathor and the spirit of a province: kingship shown as a team.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Each triad is a slab of dark greywacke with three figures standing against a back slab. The king, usually in the middle, wears the tall White Crown and steps forward; Hathor wears cow horns around a sun disc; the third figure carries the emblem of a province on the head.
story:
In 1908 George Reisner, digging for Harvard and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, cleared Menkaure's valley temple at Giza. The king had not lived to finish it, and it was completed largely in mud brick. In its rooms Reisner found the triads: Menkaure with Hathor, 'Mistress of the Sycamore', and a figure personifying one of Egypt's provinces, which the Greeks called nomes. Each wears its emblem: a jackal, a hare, the emblem of the cow goddess Bat, the sceptre of Thebes.

Finds were divided, so some triads are in Cairo and others in Boston, together with the famous pair statue of Menkaure and his queen, usually identified as Khamerernebty II. Some scholars thought there was once a triad for every province; others think only a handful were made.

The message is practical as well as religious: the provinces feed the king's cult forever, under Hathor's protection. Herodotus, who calls him Mycerinus, remembered a gentle king after harsh ones. An oracle gave him six years to live, so he lit lamps and partied every night to turn six years into twelve.
details: Hathor's headdress: cow horns cradling a sun disc. Look for her arm around the king or her hand in his.
The third figure's head: a province emblem. Jackal, the cow-faced Bat emblem or a Theban sceptre?
The king's pose: left foot forward, fists clenched, tall White Crown of the south.
The stone left between legs and behind bodies: the figures were never fully freed from the block.
fun_fact: Herodotus heard that Menkaure, told he had six years left, partied by lamplight every night to make six years into twelve.
narration: Three figures stand shoulder to shoulder in dark greywacke, and this is how a pharaoh liked to be seen: never alone. The king is Menkaure, owner of the third and smallest pyramid at Giza, in the tall White Crown, left foot forward. Beside him is Hathor, with cow horns cradling a sun disc. The third figure stands for one of Egypt's provinces, which the Greeks called nomes, and wears its emblem on the head: a jackal, a cow-faced emblem, or the sign of Thebes. George Reisner, digging for Harvard and Boston, found these in 1908 in Menkaure's valley temple, which the king had not lived to finish. The finds were divided, so some triads stayed in Cairo and others went to Boston, with the famous pair statue of Menkaure and his queen. The message is practical: the provinces will feed the king's cult forever, with Hathor's blessing. Herodotus, who calls him Mycerinus, heard that an oracle gave him six years to live, so he partied by lamplight every night to turn six years into twelve. Look now at the third figure's head: which province is it?

period: Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2580 BC (date debated)
summary: The man who built the Great Pyramid survives in a portrait 7.5 centimetres tall. It is the only complete statue of him we have.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Look for something smaller than your palm: a seated ivory figure 7.5 cm high, usually in a case of its own. The king wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, holds a flail against his right shoulder and rests his left hand on his knee. The feet and base are broken off.
story:
Khufu built the largest pyramid ever made, yet almost nothing of his own image survives: a few heads that might be his, fragments of statues smashed long ago. This ivory statuette is the only complete figure of him that most Egyptologists accept.

Flinders Petrie found it in 1903 at Abydos, in a storeroom of the temple of Osiris-Khentiamentiu at Kom el-Sultan, far south of Giza. It came out of the ground headless. Petrie stopped the work, offered a reward and had the debris of the room sieved. Three weeks later the head turned up.

Look at the face: round, fleshy, determined, not the calm mask of later royal sculpture. The crown has lost its back spike and front curl. On the right side of the throne, by the knee, is his Horus name, Medjedu; faint traces of the cartouche Khnum-Khufu are on the left.

Not everyone accepts the date. Zahi Hawass has argued it was made nearly 2,000 years later, in the 26th Dynasty, as a votive offering to a revered ancestor, pointing to the shape of the throne and the flail. Few have followed him, but nobody has disproved him. Herodotus, who called the king Cheops, heard that he shut the temples and forced all Egypt to labour on his pyramid. The little man in front of you does not look like a monster.
details: The Red Crown of Lower Egypt, with its back spike and front curl broken away.
The flail held against his right shoulder.
The Horus name Medjedu cut on the right side of the throne, by the knee.
The neck: the head was found three weeks after the body, after the rubble was sieved.
Scale: 7.5 cm here against about 146 m for the Great Pyramid you see on the 12th.
fun_fact: The Great Pyramid is nearly 2,000 times taller than this portrait of the man who built it.
narration: Lean in close: this little ivory king, 7.5 centimetres tall, is Khufu, the man who built the Great Pyramid. It is the only complete statue of him that most Egyptologists accept. The pyramid you will see on the 12th is nearly 2,000 times taller than its owner here. Flinders Petrie found him in 1903 at Abydos, the holy city of Osiris, far south of Giza. He came out of the ground without a head. Petrie stopped work, offered a reward, and had the rubble of the room sieved. Three weeks later, the head turned up. Look at it now. He wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, though its back spike has broken off. He holds a flail against his right shoulder, and his left hand rests on his knee. On the side of the throne, by his right knee, is his Horus name, Medjedu. The face is round, fleshy and determined, not the calm mask of later kings. Is it really from his lifetime? Most specialists say yes. Zahi Hawass has argued it was made nearly 2,000 years later as an offering to a famous ancestor, because of the shape of the throne and the flail. Few have followed him, but nobody has proved him wrong. The Greeks called Khufu Cheops, and Herodotus heard that he was a tyrant who shut the temples and worked his people to the bone. This tiny man does not look like a monster. Look now for the Horus name by his knee.

summary: A prince and his wife, painted about 4,600 years ago, with crystal eyes so alive that the men who found them are said to have fled.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Two seated statues in painted limestone, side by side, each a little over a metre tall. He has red-brown skin, a thin moustache and short dark hair; she is pale cream, in a white cloak, with a heavy wig and a flowered headband. Their names and titles are painted in black hieroglyphs on the high chair backs beside their heads.
story:
In 1871 workmen digging for Auguste Mariette at Meidum, under Albert Daninos, broke into mastaba 6, the brick tomb of Rahotep and Nofret near the collapsed pyramid of Sneferu. The story goes that when their lamps fell on two faces staring back with shining eyes, the workmen ran. The eyes are inlaid with rock crystal and quartz in copper rims, and they still catch the light.

Rahotep was a king's son, most likely of Sneferu, the first great pyramid builder, which would make him a brother of Khufu. His titles, painted beside his head, include High Priest of Ra at Heliopolis, Director of Expeditions and Overseer of Works. Nofret's title is 'King's Acquaintance', a rank at court. The couple had six children, three sons and three daughters.

The colours are almost untouched, and they show the rules of Egyptian art at their purest. Men are painted reddish brown, women a pale yellowish cream. It is a convention, not a skin chart, often explained as the ideal of the outdoor man and the indoor woman. Yet the details are startlingly real: Rahotep's moustache, the dark natural hairline showing under Nofret's thick wig, her floral diadem like the gold ones found at Giza, the cloak she pulls around her.
details: The eyes: rock crystal and quartz set in copper. Move your head and watch them catch the light.
Nofret's forehead: her own straight dark hair shows under the edge of the heavy wig.
Her headband: a diadem of painted flowers, like real gold diadems with inlays.
Rahotep's thin moustache, and his amulet on a cord round the neck.
The black hieroglyphs beside each head: names, and Rahotep's titles such as High Priest at Heliopolis.
fun_fact: Their names mean 'Ra is satisfied' and 'the beautiful one'. After 4,600 years, both still seem to apply.

His titles are painted in black beside his head: High Priest of Ra at Heliopolis, Director of Expeditions, Overseer of Works. Nofret was a lady of the court. They had six children. Now the colours. summary: Six geese painted on plaster 4,600 years ago, so precise that ornithologists can name the species, and so perfect that someone called them a fake.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. A long, low strip of painted plaster under glass. Six geese stand and graze on a pale ground with tufts of plants, three facing left and three facing right, mirrored around the centre. Look for the joins where the plaster was cut from a tomb wall.
story:
The frieze comes from the tomb chapel of Itet, wife of Prince Nefermaat, in their mastaba at Meidum, a short walk from the tomb of Rahotep and Nofret. Auguste Mariette and Luigi Vassalli found it in 1871; it was cut from the wall and reassembled in the museum. The tomb was experimental in other ways too: elsewhere in it, figures were cut deep and filled with coloured paste, a technique known from no other tomb.

The birds are real. Ornithologists recognise greylag geese and greater white-fronted geese, and the boldly patterned pair look like red-breasted geese. In 2021 Anthony Romilio argued that those did not match the living species well and might show an extinct goose; in 2022 other scientists replied that they fall within natural variation and artistic licence.

In 2015 the Italian Egyptologist Francesco Tiradritti suggested that the whole frieze was a 19th-century forgery, possibly by Vassalli himself. Zahi Hawass and other Egyptian authorities dismissed the claim at once, and the geese stayed in the museum and in the textbooks.
details: The red-breasted pair: brick-red necks with black and white patches, the birds in the extinct-goose debate.
The grey geese: greylags, the wild ancestors of the farmyard goose.
The symmetry: three birds face left, three face right.
Cracks and joins: the plaster was cut from a tomb wall in the 1870s and pieced together again.
fun_fact: One scientist wondered whether the red-breasted geese show a species that is now extinct. If so, this would be its only portrait.
